source.title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: An elaborate theory for an observational study protocol is a prespecified set of multiple predictions about how the data should look if a treatment has a causal effect. Ordered testing can prioritize the primary prediction and control the familywise Type I error rate across multiple tested predictions, but it may give limited information about lower-priority aspects of the theory. What statistical methods can assess the evidence for such an elaborate theory, including both individual predicted aspects and the fraction of the theory that is corroborated, while retaining valid multiplicity control and the prespecified priority among predictions?
accepted.context_brief: Evidence assessment for elaborate causal theories

evidence.quote: An elaborate theory is a set of multiple predictions about how the data would look if the treatment has an effect. In Fisher’s advice to use elaborate theories, one needs to make the predictions about how a treatment effect would manifest before seeing the data.

Although ordered testing of an elaborate theory has considerable advantages, one negative aspect is that although one might want to put a higher priority on certain aspects of the theory, one might want some information on all aspects. A different approach to assessing the evidence for an elaborate theory is to make inferences about the fraction of the elaborate theory that is corroborated as well as individual aspects of the theory. Further research on ways to assess the evidence for an elaborate theory would be useful.

accepted.question_text: In an observational study protocol that uses sample splitting, where a planning sample is used to choose outcomes or subgroups and a separate analysis sample is used for confirmatory testing, how should investigators choose the planning-sample fraction as a function of the total sample size, decide how many and which candidate outcomes should be carried forward from planning to analysis, and design sequential versions that allow more than one possible planning sample before committing to the final analysis sample?
accepted.context_brief: Sample splitting for observational study protocols

evidence.quote: In Section 5, we demonstrated that splitting may be a useful approach for selecting outcomes and subgroups in an observational study. Some problems that have not been well explored for the approach include (i) what is a good fraction for the planning sample based on the sample size?; (ii) how should we decide how many and which outcomes should be carried forward from the planning sample to test in the analysis sample?; and (iii) instead of just having one planning sample and one analysis sample, how can we use sequential analysis methods to allow for multiple possible planning samples before deciding on an analysis sample?

accepted.question_text: When an observational study has an insignificant primary analysis but a significant secondary analysis, and the investigators can give a plausible post hoc explanation for why the secondary finding could still be consistent with a true treatment effect, how should the study's conclusions be summarized so that abstracts and conclusion sections communicate the evidence without selectively over-interpreting the secondary result, and what empirical research is needed to understand how readers interpret such language?

evidence.quote: In the mountaintop mining study, the primary analysis yielded insignificant results but an aspect of the secondary analysis yielded significant results and we thought of a post hoc explanation for why this pattern could be consistent with a true treatment effect. How do we best summarize the conclusions of a study in this common situation? In this conclusion, did we pay too much heed to a secondary analysis finding? Did we selectively interpret the findings? It would be useful to have more empirical research on how readers interpret language in abstracts and conclusions of papers.
